content: Calcium, represented by the chemical symbol Ca and atomic number 20, is a soft, gray alkaline earth metal. It is the fifth most abundant element in the Earth's crust and plays a critical role in the physiology of living organisms, particularly in cellular processes. Calcium is also the most common metal found in many animals. The most abundant isotope of calcium, ⁴⁰Ca, has a nucleus containing 20 protons and 20 neutrons. This isotope is the heaviest stable isotope of any element with an equal number of protons and neutrons. Calcium is synthesized in supernova explosions through reactions involving carbon and helium nuclei (alpha particles), eventually forming the most common calcium isotope. By mass, calcium is the seventh most common element in Earth's oceans. Chemically, calcium is reactive and moderately soft for a metal, though harder than lead. It can be cut with a knife, albeit with difficulty. In its pure form, calcium is a silvery metallic element that must be extracted via electrolysis from fused salts like calcium chloride. Upon exposure to air, it rapidly forms a gray-white coating of calcium oxide and calcium nitride. Calcium is somewhat challenging to ignite, similar to magnesium, but when it burns, it produces an intense red light. Calcium reacts with water, releasing hydrogen gas at a noticeable rate, though not rapidly enough at room temperature to generate significant heat. This reaction is slowed by the formation of an insoluble white layer of calcium hydroxide on the metal's surface. In acidic water solutions where the resulting salt is soluble, calcium reacts vigorously. Calcium salts and ionic solutions of calcium (Ca²⁺) are colorless, and many calcium salts are insoluble in water. The taste of calcium ions varies, being described as mildly salty, sour, mineral-like, or even soothing. Many animals can detect calcium through taste, using this ability to locate sources like salt licks. In human nutrition, soluble calcium salts can be added to tart juices without significantly altering their taste. Calcium is the fifth most abundant element in the human body by mass. It serves as a vital cellular ionic messenger with numerous functions and acts as a structural component in bones. The relatively high atomic number of calcium in the skeleton makes bones radio-opaque. After the human body is dried (e.g., through cremation), approximately one-third of the remaining solid mass is calcium, primarily from the skeleton, which contains about one kilogram of calcium on average. The rest of the mass is mostly phosphorus and oxygen. Applications of Calcium Compounds Calcium cyclamate (Ca(C₆H₁₁NHSO₄)₂): Previously used as a sweetening agent but is now banned due to suspected carcinogenic properties. Calcium gluconate (Ca(C₆H₁₁O₇)₂): Used as a food additive and in vitamin supplements. Calcium permanganate (Ca(MnO₄)₂): Utilized in liquid rocket propellants, textile production, water sterilization, and dental procedures. Calcium phosphate (Ca₃(PO₄)₂): Used as an animal feed supplement, fertilizer, in dough and yeast production, glass manufacturing, and dental products. Calcium tungstate (CaWO₄): Found in luminous paints, fluorescent lights, and X-ray studies. Nutrition Calcium is an essential component of a healthy diet, necessary for the growth and maintenance of bones and teeth. Calcium requirements must be met throughout life to prevent deficiencies. Long-term calcium deficiency can lead to osteoporosis, a condition characterized by bone deterioration and an increased risk of fractures. While chronic calcium deficits can impair bone and tooth formation, excessive calcium retention can result in hypercalcemia, which may impair kidney function and reduce the absorption of other minerals. High calcium intake was once thought to contribute to kidney stone formation, but recent studies suggest that dietary calcium may actually reduce this risk. Vitamin D is required for calcium absorption. Dairy products, such as milk and cheese, are well-known sources of calcium. However, individuals with dairy allergies, lactose intolerance, or those who avoid dairy for ethical or health reasons (e.g., vegans) may need alternative sources. Non-dairy calcium sources include seaweeds (kelp, wakame, hijiki), nuts and seeds (almonds, sesame), blackstrap molasses, beans, oranges, amaranth, collard greens, okra, rutabaga, broccoli, dandelion leaves, kale, sardines, and fortified products like orange juice and soy milk. Eggshells, when ground into a powder, can also serve as a calcium source. The calcium content of most foods is available in the USDA National Nutrient Database. Dietary Calcium Supplements Calcium supplements are used to prevent and treat calcium deficiencies. Experts recommend taking no more than 500 mg of calcium at a time, as absorption efficiency decreases with higher doses. It is advised to spread doses throughout the day, with the last dose taken near bedtime. Recommended daily calcium intake ranges from 1000 to 1500 mg, depending on life stage. Calcium carbonate: The most common and least expensive supplement, containing 40% elemental calcium. It is best taken with food to aid absorption but may cause gas and constipation in some individuals. Magnesium can help alleviate these side effects. Some calcium carbonate supplements include added vitamin D to enhance absorption. Calcium citrate: Contains 21% elemental calcium and is easier to digest than calcium carbonate, with a lower risk of causing gas or constipation. However, it is more expensive and requires larger doses to achieve the same calcium intake. Calcium phosphate: More expensive than calcium carbonate but less so than calcium citrate. It is easily absorbed and less likely to cause digestive issues. Calcium lactate and calcium aspartate: These are more expensive and harder to digest than calcium carbonate. Calcium chelates: Chemically bonded with agents recognized by the body as food, these forms are better absorbed than other calcium types. Examples include citrate, malate, and aspartate. Dicalcium malate, a newer chelate form, contains 30% elemental calcium. Prevention of Fractures Due to Osteoporosis Studies on calcium's role in preventing fractures often examine combinations of calcium and vitamin D rather than calcium alone. Results have been mixed, with some trials showing benefits and others not. Variations in outcomes may be due to differences in calcium doses and baseline calcium intake in control groups. However, increasing calcium intake is known to promote bone calcium deposition, which is more effective in preventing vertebral compression fractures caused by osteoporosis than in preventing cortical bone fractures at the hip and wrist. Potential Role in Cancer Prevention A meta-analysis by the Cochrane Collaboration of two randomized controlled trials suggested that calcium might moderately help prevent adenomatous colonic polyps. However, more recent studies have produced conflicting results.
